title: Bad conscience, bruised pride, and the twinge before
core: All three name a private, uncomfortable feeling triggered by your own conduct or your own showing — the inward wince rather than anger at someone else. They split on two axes: **when** the feeling arrives (before the act or after it), and **what is injured** (your conscience or your dignity). Because all three are polite, restrained, formal-register words, English speakers reach for them interchangeably when they shouldn't — one of them involves no wrongdoing at all.

words.nuance: The only one that arrives **before** the deed, and the only one small enough to be overridden — a flicker you can act straight through. It's also the only one usually measured by its absence: "had no qualms about firing them" grades someone's scruples, not their feelings.

The only one that concedes actual fault and faces outward, toward the person wronged — defences down, excuses withdrawn. It's the strongest of the three and the one others read off you (you *look* contrite), which is why it can be faked and why "suitably contrite" is nearly always sardonic.

The only one where nothing wrong was done — your **pride** took the hit, not your conscience: outclassed, proved wrong, publicly wrong-footed. It's swallowed rather than displayed, and in its home phrase "much to my chagrin" the speaker is usually being wry about their own vanity.

exam_note: The classic trap is treating **chagrin** as a guilt word: GRE sentences use it where the subject is merely embarrassed at being outdone, so a guilt/remorse answer choice fits the mood but not the meaning — and watch **qualm** appear negated, where the sentence is characterizing a person's ruthlessness, not their emotion.
